caption:
Was the Cardiff Giant real? No. It was carved in 1868.

On October 16, 1869, workers digging a well behind William C. Newell's barn in Cardiff, New York, hit a ten-foot stone man. Newell put a tent over it and charged fifty cents for a fifteen-minute viewing. Three to five hundred people a day came, and the town's hotels and restaurants had their best four days ever.

Newell's cousin George Hull, a tobacconist, had arranged all of it. After losing an argument at a Methodist revival about the giants in Genesis 6:4, he paid men to quarry a gypsum block at Fort Dodge, Iowa, telling them it was for a Lincoln monument. It was carved in Chicago in the shape of Hull's own body. He left off the hair, because a geologist told him hair does not petrify. Sand, sulphuric acid and steel knitting needles aged the surface and faked the pores. Cost: $2,600.

Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh called it "a most decided humbug" — fresh tool marks on soluble gypsum that had supposedly lain in wet earth for centuries. Hull confessed on December 10, 1869. On February 2, 1870, a court declared both his giant and P. T. Barnum's unauthorized plaster copy fakes.

Still unresolved: whether Edward Burkhardt, the Chicago stonecutter who took the job, knew what he was making. And "there's a sucker born every minute" was said by syndicate head David Hannum, not Barnum — the misattribution has never come off.

Images: the giant photographed by Bain News Service in 1910; the lithograph "The Onondaga Giant"; and an 1873 stereocard of the Fort Dodge gypsum quarry, front and back, from the New York Public Library.

cards.headline: Ten feet of stone man, <y>found behind a barn</y>
cards.note: Workers digging a well hit it on October 16, 1869.
cards.alt: Glass negative of a large pale stone figure lying in a dug pit beside a tree root..

cards.headline: A souvenir print listed <y>every measurement</y>
cards.note: Whole length 10 feet 4½ inches. Length of nose, 6 inches. Width of palm, 7 inches. It weighed 2,990 pounds.
cards.alt: Lithograph of a reclining nude stone figure on a plinth, drawn in soft grey tones.

cards.headline: The back of a stereocard <y>names the two men</y>
cards.note: Printed in 1873: the block was taken from this quarry to Chicago, carved, shipped to New York, buried in a barn lot and "discovered". The perpetrators were George Hull and H. B. Martin.
cards.source: Stereocard verso, 1873 · New York Public Library
cards.alt: Printed text on the pink back of a stereocard describing the Cardiff Giant imposture.

cards.headline: It started as <y>a block of gypsum</y> in Iowa
cards.note: In 1868 Hull hired men at Fort Dodge to quarry a block ten feet four and a half inches long. He told them it was for a monument to Abraham Lincoln.
cards.source: Cardiff Glen, Iowa, 1873 · New York Public Library
cards.alt: Faded albumen view of a pale rock face in woodland above a heap of broken stone.

cards.headline: <y>Fresh tool marks</y> on soluble gypsum
cards.note: Yale paleontologist Othniel C. Marsh said gypsum buried for centuries in wet earth could not keep fresh tool marks. He called the giant "a most decided humbug".
cards.alt: Close view of the stone giant's hairless head and shoulder, pitted and stained.

cards.headline: <y>He confessed proudly</y>, then the court agreed
cards.note: Hull talked on December 10, 1869. On February 2, 1870, both his giant and Barnum's copy were ruled fakes. What the records do not settle: whether the Chicago stonecutter knew what the job was for.
cards.source: Cardiff Glen, Iowa, 1873 · New York Public Library
cards.alt: Second half of an 1873 stereo view: quarried rock wall, trees, scattered stone blocks.
